Your teacher covers these two ideas in class, and these questions check you've got the basics: what makes a good key, and why the way we classify keeps changing.

## Building a key

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Node 4 (constructing keys): binary, observable questions; a key for n organisms needs n - 1 questions; testing by a peer shows faults."
tasks:
  - check: {"type":"sort","q":"Would this make a good question in a key?","options":["Good question","Poor question"],"items":[["Does it have six legs?","Good question"],["Does it have feathers?","Good question"],["Is it large?","Poor question","\"Large\" depends on who is judging, so two people could answer differently."],["Is it scary?","Poor question","That's an opinion, and not something you can observe."],["Does it have a shell?","Good question"]]}
    hint: ["Would two different people always answer this question the same way when they look at the same animal?", "Think about whether you could settle each question just by looking closely, or by counting something."]
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"You build a key to identify 6 different organisms. About how many questions does it need?","options":["5: each question splits one group into two","6: one per organism","3: half the number of organisms","12: two per organism"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"Close, but the last organism doesn't need a question of its own, so count again.","Each question only splits one group into two, so three questions can't separate six organisms.","Each question already has two answers, so you don't need two questions for every organism."],"explain":"Each question splits one group into two, so to end with 6 separate organisms you make 5 splits."}
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"A classmate follows your key and names a specimen wrongly. What does that tell you?","options":["Your key has a fault, such as an unclear question or a wrong branch, to find and fix","The classmate is not good at science","The specimen is not in the key","Keys cannot be made accurate"],"answer":0,"explain":"Testing with another person shows up unclear questions that you couldn't see yourself."}
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"A key ends with the question \"Does it have four legs?\" to separate a dog from a cat. What is wrong with it?","options":["Both answers are yes, so the question doesn't split them: it needs a feature only one of them has","The key needs more animals in it","Legs are not an observable feature","Nothing: both animals reaching the same end is fine"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"More animals won't fix a question that doesn't split the two it has.","You can see legs, so observability isn't the issue; think about how each animal would answer.","Each organism has to end up at its own name, or the key can't identify anything."],"explain":"Every question must split the group into two, so pick a feature one animal has and the other doesn't, such as \"Does it have retractable claws?\""}
    hint: "If you asked this question about a dog and then about a cat, would they end up in different places?"
  - check: {"type":"reflect","text":"I can write yes/no questions about features I can see, and I know a peer test shows me faults in my key."}
```

## Classification changes

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Node 5 (change over time): a real reclassification with its evidence, and why change strengthens confidence in science."
tasks:
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"Which is a real example of classification changing because of new evidence?","options":["DNA comparisons showed that archaea are not bacteria, so a third domain of life was recognised","A scientist preferred a different name, so the group was renamed","An animal changed its features during its life, so it was moved to a new group","Two groups looked alike, so they were merged without any new evidence"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"Groups change because of new evidence, and a scientist's preference isn't enough.","Classification is about a species and its relatives rather than one animal's life, and species are reclassified when new evidence shows how they're related.","Looking alike isn't enough, because a change needs evidence about relationships."],"explain":"Comparing DNA (and other molecules) showed that archaea are a separate line of life, not part of the bacteria. Fungi were also moved: DNA shows they are closer relatives of animals than of plants."}
  - check: {"type":"sort","q":"Could this lead scientists to change a classification?","options":["Can change it","Cannot change it"],"items":[["New DNA evidence","Can change it"],["A better microscope showing new structures","Can change it"],["A newly discovered species that does not fit","Can change it"],["An opinion with no evidence","Cannot change it","Science changes when there's new evidence, not just because someone has a new opinion."],["Wanting the groups to look neat","Cannot change it"]]}
  - check: {"type":"question","q":"Scientists reclassified some organisms. Does that make science less trustworthy?","options":["No: updating ideas when new evidence appears is how science works, and it makes the ideas more reliable","Yes: it shows scientists were wrong about everything","Yes: classification should never change","It makes no difference to how reliable it is"],"answer":0,"feedback":[null,"Most of the classification still stands, and the new evidence only improved some parts.","Ideas that are fixed and can't respond to evidence are less reliable, not more.","It does make a difference, so think about which way it cuts."],"explain":"Science corrects itself, and because ideas are tested against new evidence, the ones that survive can be trusted more."}
    hint: ["Think about what made the scientists change the classification, and what they were responding to.", "Ask whether the old groups were thrown out completely, or only the parts the new evidence showed up."]
  - check: {"type":"reflect","text":"I can give a real example of classification changing and the evidence that changed it, and say why change makes science stronger."}
```

```teacher
summary: A self-test on constructing dichotomous keys and on classification
  changing over time (AC9S7U01, nodes 4 and 5, both hinge nodes taught in
  class).
time: 12
timing: Node 4 6 min · Node 5 6 min
goals:
  - I can say what makes a good key question.
  - I can say how many questions a key for six organisms needs.
  - I can give an example of classification changing and the evidence behind it.
before: >
  A Quick check: a few questions on what students should know for AC9S7U01 nodes
  4 and 5, which you teach in class. It has no board, no clip and no new
  teaching, and it is optional, so it never holds up course completion. Set the
  width with `?width=minimum`, `typical` (default) or `wider`.


  Use it as a self-test after your teaching, a starter, or revision. Node 4 is
  best done with real specimens or cards; the questions only check the basics.
  For node 5 the reclassification examples are fungi nearer to animals than
  plants, protists as several lineages, and archaea as a separate domain.
running:
  - "Node 4: students first make a key for six objects on the bench, then do the
    sort."
  - "Node 5: ask for one reclassification example before they answer; the
    question lists a real one."
struggle: Questions a stranger could answer the same way. When a student writes
  "is it big?", ask whether two people would agree.
stuck:
  - see: A student writes "is it pretty?" or "is it large?" in a key.
    ask: Would two people always answer the same way?
    fix: Use features you can observe and count, such as legs, wings or a shell.
  - see: A student thinks scientists changing a classification means they were
      wrong.
    ask: What made them change it?
    fix: New evidence. Science updates with evidence, which is why it can be
      trusted.
stretch: Make a key for the six students nearest you using only features you can
  see. Swap with a neighbour and mark where it fails.
support: Give half-finished keys to complete, and a list of observable features
  to choose from.
leads: >
  Back in class: swap keys for peer testing; discuss the Wider lenses (First
  Nations classification, microscopes, biosecurity).
exit:
  q: Why must a key question be about something you can observe?
  a: So anyone can answer it the same way and reach the same organism.
explain: >
  A good key question has **two answers** and is about a feature you can
  **observe**. Each question splits a group in two, so a key for 6 organisms
  needs 5 questions.


  Classification changes when there is **new evidence** (DNA, better
  microscopes, new species). That makes science more reliable, not less.
```
